prize_parts.citation: For establishing nominal rigidities as the foundation of modern monetary-policy analysis: staggered price and contract setting, policy rules, and a microfounded framework for monetary policy.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged in parts and names, but I hold it with a clearer view of what it rests on. The case is conceptual centrality and institutional reach. Calvo supplies the tractable staggered-pricing mechanism that gives the New Keynesian Phillips curve its form. Taylor supplies staggered contracts and the interest-rate rule as a benchmark for policy. Woodford integrates these into a microfounded framework for evaluating monetary policy. The work is 25 to 45 years old and has been run through the 2008 crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. It was modified in those episodes and not abandoned, and it remains the common language of central-bank analysis. This strand has not been recognised directly by earlier prizes. The chair asked whether my own micro evidence on price adjustment weakens Calvo's claim. I concluded that it does not change the names. Survey and transaction-level evidence, including my own work on Swedish firms, gasoline retail prices and asymmetric adjustment, points to state-dependent behaviour. That qualifies the literal realism of time-dependent pricing, but it does not remove Calvo's role as the originator of the building block that the framework and its critics both use. Swapping Gali for Calvo or Taylor would not escape the critique either, because the New Keynesian Phillips curve Gali developed rests on Calvo pricing. I count the micro evidence as a cost to the framework's literal assumptions, and as no argument for a different trio. I do not take agreement among B012 supporters on the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio as independent evidence of merit. Those four files share premises, and the chair is a co-author of mine.
statement.case_against: The credit is diffuse, and the Committee has not resolved the attribution problem in this round. Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler made major theoretical, empirical and quantitative contributions that make the framework usable, and any three-person cut omits some of them. Taylor's claim leans on his staggered-contracts work, because the rule alone is a thin basis. The micro evidence on state-dependent adjustment is a real scientific qualification of Calvo's mechanism, and I have not tested it against the full literature. The framework's record after 2008 and 2021, and the shift toward heterogeneous-agent models, leave room for a reasonable view that this case is less settled than B026's. B026 has cleaner attribution and over twenty years of firm-level confirmation, and B007 has the cleanest two-author credit. If the Committee weights attribution cleanliness more heavily than breadth of influence, B026 is a defensible first choice, and I would not regard that outcome as a weak one.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B012 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He concedes that the Taylor rule is closer to a rule of thumb than to a deep theorem, that Gali would be an acceptable substitute, and that B007 and B026 have cleaner attribution.
responses.response: I agree that the rule alone would be thin, and the chair's question about Gali for Taylor is fair. I would not object to Gali in place of Taylor if colleagues find the empirical bridge more persuasive than the staggered-contracts priority. I would not replace Calvo with Gali, because the New Keynesian Phillips curve builds on Calvo pricing and the originator should be credited. I also note that you and I are co-authors (IJIO 2026) and share a first choice. Neither fact should be read as independent evidence for the trio.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B026 first with Melitz and Helpman. She argues that selection and reallocation across firms is a distinct advance from the 2008 prize, that it has been confirmed on firm-level data across many countries, and that Redding's work is more derivative.
responses.response: I find this the strongest competing case, and B026 remains my first alternative. I accept your distinctness argument, and Melitz-Helpman is a fair reading of the originating theory. From my work on exporters' pricing and invoicing I would add one caution. Exporter-premium facts and the quantitative-trade line (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum) are not credited on this ballot entry, so a citation should name the theoretical framework and should not claim to honour all firm-level trade research. Your Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple argument convinces me on the pair. My reason for keeping B012 ahead is breadth of institutional influence, which I weigh against its weaker attribution, and I do not treat support counts as merit.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B007 first with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He says the mechanism is a conceptual discovery with about thirty years of follow-up. He also grants that B012's credit is diffuse and that omitting Calvo or the Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans line is a weakness.
responses.response: I accept the attribution weakness. I also agree that Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean and original two-author mechanism, and your move from three names to the pair strengthens the case. My remaining reasons for ranking it below B012 are narrower scope and closeness to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises. The empirical identification of collateral channels is also weaker than the theory, as you and Boppart both concede. That is a difference of degree, and I would not call B007 an unreasonable choice. On Christiano-Eichenbaum-Evans, I treat estimation of medium-scale models as a distinct achievement from the core theory, and under the three-person cap I would not combine them.

responses.point: Strömberg proposes a two-part prize: Kiyotaki and Moore (B007) plus Melitz alone (B026). He acknowledges that the one-person B026 part may look like a product of the three-laureate cap and that he would prefer to name Helpman.
responses.response: I respect the reasoning, and the two parts do reflect your standard of a sharp mechanism and a framework tied to firm-level evidence. I would not prefer this configuration. A Melitz-only part reads as an artefact of the cap, and omitting Helpman weakens the attribution that makes B026 attractive. Two parts also split three people across unrelated fields without a shared scientific argument. If the Committee wants B026, I would support Melitz and Helpman as a single part, as you say you would. I would treat that as a separate configuration from mine. I do not see the combined award as a compromise that resolves the disagreement over merit.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B007 first with the pair and argues that Kiyotaki-Moore is distinct from the 2022 prize because it does not require a bank run or intermediary failure. He also notes the post-2020 inflation as a recent test of the New Keynesian framework.
responses.response: The distinctness argument is persuasive. A collateral-driven feedback between asset values and borrowing is a different mechanism from runs and deposit insurance, and I accept that the 2022 overlap is smaller than it first looks. I still treat it as a cost relative to a strand no prize has covered. On the 2021-23 inflation, I would qualify your framing as Andersson did. It tests the framework's forecasting and policy use, and the observed pattern points to modification, such as nonlinear price adjustment and supply shocks. It does not by itself settle the conceptual question of who originated the core elements.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee will decide that the discovery is the origination of nominal-rigidity mechanisms (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) or the usable policy framework, which would shift weight toward Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler.

How much the micro evidence on state-dependent and asymmetric price adjustment should reduce the credit given to time-dependent pricing. I have not independently verified this against the full literature, and my own research area could bias my reading either way.
How to weigh the post-2008 and 2021-23 performance critiques and the shift toward heterogeneous-agent models against the framework's institutional influence.

Whether attribution cleanliness (B026, B007) should outrank breadth of influence (B012), and whether a Melitz-Helpman pair is premature given the uncredited Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum contributions.
Whether the Kiyotaki-Moore pair is distinct enough from the 2022 prize, and whether a wider macro-finance award adding Gertler is preferable.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My research on price setting and menu costs, including the 2026 IJIO paper co-authored with Hassler and Ellingsen, is close to the nominal-rigidities literature in B012, although it is not work of any credited candidate. My chair co-author, who is a committee member, prefers the same trio, and I do not treat that agreement as independent evidence. My work on exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency and the law of one price lies near B026, which is only an alternative here. My IO background is close to B024, which is not in my configuration. None of my listed co-authors appears among the credited names on B012, B026 or B007. My spouse is a former prime minister, which is a public fact, and the profile shows no evidence that it bears on any candidate. I disclose these connections without adjudicating them.
